source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"An elevated PSA is not diagnostic by itself; prostate cancer can raise PSA, but benign enlargement, inflammation, and other factors can also increase it.","B":"An elevated PSA confirms prostate cancer by itself because benign prostate conditions and recent prostate inflammation do not meaningfully affect the result.","C":"An elevated PSA has no established clinical relevance because prostate cells do not normally produce PSA and cancer does not alter serum concentrations.","D":"An elevated PSA is considered normal in every man over age 50 regardless of the actual value, symptoms, examination, medications, or prior results."}}
source_row.rationale: PSA is produced by normal and malignant prostate cells, and elevated values can occur with prostate cancer as well as benign conditions such as BPH and prostatitis. Option A is correct because an elevated PSA requires clinical interpretation and possible further evaluation rather than serving as a stand-alone diagnosis. Option B overstates specificity. Option C is false. Option D incorrectly applies an age-based blanket rule.
source_row.source_detail: National Cancer Institute — Prostate-Specific Antigen (PSA) Test Fact Sheet: PSA is produced by normal and malignant prostate cells; levels can rise with prostate cancer but also with benign prostatic hyperplasia, prostatitis/inflammation, and other factors, so an elevated PSA alone does not diagnose prostate cancer. Current NCI PSA Fact Sheet live-rechecked 2026-08-15; difficulty corrected to easy because the item tests direct interpretation of a nonspecific tumor marker rather than multistep clinical judgment. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Physiological Integrity — Reduction of Risk Potential: diagnostic probability tools, laboratory/tumor-marker interpretation, ECG/lab monitoring and potential complications. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

source_row.stem: A client has an elevated prostate-specific antigen (PSA) result and assumes this confirms prostate cancer. Which explanation is most accurate?
